title: Greet first (Avot 4:15)
hook: the person who just beat you walks in: Matya ben Charash says be first to greet everyone; better a lion's tail than a fox's head
tomorrow: the hallway before the curtain. what do you do there?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabbi Yannai: we can't explain why the wicked thrive or the good suffer. Not in our hands. Today, the same mishnah, and something that is.

She beat you. The job, the part, the spot on the team. And now she's walking into the same room, and there's a half second where somebody has to say hi first. Do you? Rabbi Matya ben Charash says yes, and not only to her. Be first to greet every person. Then he adds a line about lions and foxes, and that's where the argument starts.
screen: `SHE BEAT YOU.` → `WHO SAYS HI FIRST?` → `LIONS AND FOXES.`

segments.voice: First, the greeting. Be first to greet every person. Not every person who greets you, not every person on your side. Every person. The Talmud says of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai that nobody ever greeted him first, not even a stranger in the market. That's one to tell a friend tonight: the Talmud remembers a sage who always got the hello in first. Then Matya's second line. Be a tail to lions, rather than a head to foxes. His best case: put yourself where the people are stronger than you, even at the back. You'll learn more trailing great people than leading small ones. Now the other voice, from the same book. Back in chapter two, Hillel says: in a place where there are no people, try to be a person. His best case: sometimes the room needs a head, and nobody else is stepping up. Staying a tail somewhere grand can be a way of hiding. Notice they're not opposites. Matya is talking about where to go to grow. Hillel is talking about what to do where you already are. Avot keeps both. And the greeting fits either way. The tail greets first. So does the head. Greet first.
screen: `BE FIRST TO GREET EVERY PERSON.` · `NOBODY GREETED HIM FIRST.` · `MATYA: A TAIL TO LIONS.` · `HILLEL: WHERE NO ONE IS, BE SOMEONE.` · then, large: `GREET FIRST.`

segments.voice: Say one plain greeting out loud, softly: hi, or good morning, or shalom, the way you'd say it first to someone walking in. Then, for the rest of the sit, bring to mind one person you usually wait to be greeted by, and say it to them, silently, first.
screen: `SAY ONE GREETING OUT LOUD.` · `ONE PERSON YOU WAIT FOR.` · `GREET THEM FIRST, SILENTLY.`

segments.voice: Greet first. Rabbi Matya ben Charash: be first to greet every person, and be a tail to lions rather than a head to foxes.
Your line for today: greet first, whoever walks in the door. Thirty-nine of sixty, said first.

screen: `DAY 1466 COUNTS.` → `AVOT, CHAPTERS 3–6 · 39 OF 60.` → `TOMORROW: THE HALLWAY BEFORE THE CURTAIN. WHAT DO YOU DO THERE?`

howItsDone: Many Jews greet with shalom, peace, or shalom aleichem, peace be upon you, answered aleichem shalom; Avot's saying makes being first to offer it a practice.

match.prompt: two voices in Avot — tap the pairs.
pairs: where no one is, try to be someone

myth: Matya says greet first only the people who greet you
be first to greet every person, he says.
the Talmud says nobody ever greeted Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai first
not even a stranger in the market.
Matya and Hillel flatly contradict each other
Matya speaks of where to go to grow; Hillel of what to do where no one leads. Avot keeps both.

fork.setup: your cousin can join a famous lab as the most junior intern, or lead the science club at her small school, where no one else will. she's leaning toward the club. make Hillel's best case for her.
options: where no one is stepping up, being the one who leads is its own kind of growth.
being the head of anything always beats being the tail of something great.
famous labs are full of foxes, so the small club is wiser anyway.
fork.reveal: Hillel: in a place where there are no people, try to be a person. that's his case, not a ranking. Matya's case for the lab is just as real.

original.note: Hebrew: first with the greeting of peace, from Matya's 'be first to greet every person'.

trapdoor: what you thought: be polite and say hello.
what it means: greet every person first, whoever they are; and choose where to grow, a tail among lions, without forgetting Hillel's call to step up where no one does.
what a scholar hears: the greeting is shalom, peace, and the Talmud's story of Yochanan ben Zakkai makes 'greet first' a mark of a great sage.
guess: be the first to offer a greeting to anyone you meet
greet your elders before you greet anyone younger
say good morning before you speak to God each day
recall: we can't explain why the good suffer

chat.says: lena's at the cast party tonight. she got districts over me. do i really have to say hi first?
options: Say hi first. Matya means every person, not just those who beat you.
Wait for her to come over. She won, so it's on her to say hi first.
Skip the party; avoiding her is kinder than a fake hello tonight.
chat.meaning: Be first to greet every person. A greeting isn't a verdict on who deserved to win; it's shalom, offered first.

Matya ben Charash.meaning: a sage of the Mishnah; today's saying is his

Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai.meaning: a great sage and teacher, praised in the Talmud for greeting first

Hillel.meaning: an early sage of Avot, known for patience and kindness

Talmud.meaning: the rabbis' vast discussion of the Mishnah

sources.ref: Mishnah Avot 4:15 (Rabbi Matya ben Charash: be first to greet every person; be a tail to lions rather than a head to foxes)
Mishnah Avot 2:5 (Hillel: in a place where there are no people, strive to be a person)
Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 17a (no one ever greeted Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai first, not even a non-Jew in the market)
